prompts.prompt: what is the difference between precision and recall?
sketch: Confusion counts with example numbers: true positives, false positives, false negatives (and true negatives).
Precision = TP / (TP + FP) and recall = TP / (TP + FN), each computed from those same counts.

prompts.prompt: what does the sigmoid activation function do?
sketch: x axis: input z, about -6 to 6; y axis: sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + e^-z), an S-curve from 0 to 1.
It passes 0.5 at z = 0 and flattens near 0 and 1 (saturation).

prompts.prompt: what is gini impurity
sketch: x axis: the share p of one class in a node, 0 to 1; y axis: Gini impurity 1 - (p^2 + (1-p)^2) = 2p(1-p): 0 at p = 0 and 1, peak 0.5 at p = 0.5.
Or bars of one node's class shares, with the impurity 1 - (sum of squared shares) stated and computed from those bars.

prompts.prompt: what is cross entropy
sketch: x axis: predicted probability of the true class, 0 to 1; y axis: loss -ln(p), very large near 0 and 0 at p = 1.
Or bars of the true distribution next to the predicted one, with H(p, q) = -sum p log q computed from the bar values.

prompts.prompt: what is a learning rate schedule?
sketch: x axis: training step or epoch; y axis: learning rate falling over training (step decay, exponential decay or cosine; a warm-up rising first if named).
The plotted values follow the schedule formula the prose states (for example lr_t = lr_0 * gamma^t).

prompts.prompt: what is gradient descent?
sketch: x axis: a parameter w; y axis: the loss L(w), a bowl; steps move downhill toward the minimum.
Each step is w <- w - eta * dL/dw: the learning rate eta times the slope sets the step size.

prompts.prompt: what does softmax do?
sketch: Before: raw scores (logits) such as 2.0, 1.0, 0.1; after: probabilities e^z_i / sum_j e^z_j, about 0.66, 0.24, 0.10.
The outputs are all positive and sum to 1; the largest score keeps the largest share.

prompts.prompt: what happens when I send an email?
prompts.why: Your client, your mail server, the recipient server and their client pass the message along: a sequence. Digital: no picture.

prompts.prompt: how does a DNS lookup work?
prompts.why: Resolver, root, TLD and authoritative servers exchange queries and answers: a sequence.

prompts.prompt: compare a stack and a queue
prompts.why: Two structures with different orders (LIFO vs FIFO): one diagram each (a stack as layers, a queue as a sequence/flow), or a comparison plus one.

prompts.prompt: what is the difference between depth-first and breadth-first search?
prompts.why: Two traversal orders over the same tree: two diagrams, or a comparison plus a tree.

prompts.prompt: how do arrays and linked lists store data differently?
prompts.why: Contiguous cells vs nodes linked by pointers: one diagram of each.

prompts.prompt: how does a plant cell look different from an animal cell?
prompts.why: Two appearances (cell wall, chloroplasts, vacuole vs none): two pictures, or the cell figure plus a picture or comparison.

prompts.prompt: how does a solar eclipse happen?
prompts.why: Spatial geometry (Sun, Moon, Earth in a line, the shadow); no diagram kind draws positions.

prompts.prompt: how does a four-stroke car engine work?
prompts.why: The cylinder and piston are an object to see; intake, compression, power, exhaust is a cycle.

prompts.prompt: how does a robot arm pick up an object?
prompts.why: A physical machine doing something: picture plus the sense-plan-grip steps.

prompts.prompt: what are the parts of a medieval castle?
prompts.why: A place: the learner needs to see the walls, keep, gatehouse and moat in one scene. A part tree is a fair second.

prompts.prompt: explain leaf venation
prompts.why: Vein patterns (net vs parallel) are visual; two pictures or one picture side by side is the answer.

prompts.prompt: explain a 3D mesh
prompts.why: A mesh is a shape: the learner needs to see a wireframe surface of triangles. A vertex/edge/face relationship diagram is a fair second visual; a stack of bands is not what a mesh is.

prompts.prompt: how does a volcano erupt?
prompts.why: The volcano and its magma chamber are a place to see; the eruption is a process.

prompts.prompt: how does the human heart pump blood?
prompts.why: Anatomy (a picture of the heart's chambers) plus the blood route (cycle or flow) is the full answer; either alone still teaches part of it.

prompts.prompt: how does a suspension bridge hold up its deck?
prompts.why: A structure to see (towers, main cables, hangers, deck); the load path is a fair diagram second or alone.

prompts.prompt: what are the parts of a transformer block?
sketch: Input embeddings -> multi-head self-attention -> add & layer norm -> feed-forward network -> add & layer norm.
Residual connections skip around the attention and around the feed-forward network.
prompts.relabel: 2026-11-09 owner: the new kinds were built for this prompt (block-stack)

prompts.prompt: how are attention weights computed?
sketch: Scores: the query dotted with every key, divided by sqrt(d_k); softmax turns one query's scores into weights that sum to 1.
The output is the weighted sum of the value vectors; a larger weight means that token contributes more.

prompts.prompt: how does a hash table work?
prompts.why: Keys hashed to buckets: relationship/flow/transformation (or a bucket matrix).

prompts.prompt: how does tokenization work?
prompts.why: Text becomes a list of tokens: transformation, or the steps as a flow.

prompts.prompt: what is overfitting?
sketch: x axis: model complexity or training time; training error keeps falling while validation error falls, then rises.
The gap after the turning point is overfitting: the model fits noise in the training data.

prompts.prompt: how does merge sort work?
prompts.why: Split then merge: a tree of halves or a before/after transformation.

prompts.prompt: how does RAG work?
prompts.why: Query -> retriever -> documents -> model -> answer, between named parts: sequence or flow.

prompts.prompt: how does backpropagation work?
prompts.why: Forward pass, loss, gradients flowing back through the layers, weight update: a flow (or the training loop as a cycle, the chain rule as relationship).

prompts.prompt: what is a random forest?
prompts.why: Word collision: many decision trees that vote; never a picture of a forest.

prompts.prompt: how does RLHF work?
sketch: People rank model answers -> a reward model learns those preferences -> the policy model is tuned to raise the reward.
The loop repeats with new answers and rankings; a penalty keeps the policy close to the original model.

prompts.prompt: how does the TCP handshake work?
prompts.why: Messages between two actors in order: sequence. A picture can only be decoration.

prompts.prompt: what is batch normalization?
prompts.why: Activations re-centred and re-scaled per batch: before/after transformation.

prompts.prompt: what are the layers of a neural network?
prompts.why: Word collision with 'layers': input, hidden and output layers in order; layers, flow or relationship are all right.

prompts.prompt: what is a convolutional neural network?
sketch: Image -> convolution layers (filters slide over it making feature maps) -> pooling (downsampling) -> fully connected layer -> class scores.
Early layers find edges; later layers combine them into shapes and objects.

prompts.prompt: how do the generator and discriminator in a GAN work together?
sketch: The generator turns random noise into fake samples; the discriminator labels samples real or fake.
The discriminator's feedback (its gradient) trains the generator to fool it; both improve against each other in a loop.

prompts.prompt: how did the Roman Empire rise and fall?
prompts.why: Events in time: timeline. A picture of Rome is a fair second.

prompts.prompt: Show two histograms comparing raw and log-transformed values.
sketch: Core: Two histograms of the same observations, one raw and one log-transformed, each with explicit bins; the raw one is right-skewed and the log one is more even; the transform is stated.
Optional: The transform's valid domain and the paired values.
prompts.note: Required-kind path: a comparison counts as right only when its panels are histograms; a single histogram diagram counts only if it shows both distributions (checked by hand).
